Introduction to Python Project : Personal Loan Analysis¶

Problem Statement¶

Write the problem statement and objectives here

Context

AllLife Bank is a mid-sized, fast-growing US-based financial institution that offers a range of retail banking services, including savings and checking accounts, fixed deposits, and personal loans. The bank’s business model is centered on building long-term customer relationships, expanding its retail footprint, and growing its loan portfolio to drive sustainable profitability through interest income.

It currently relies on a large base of liability customers (depositors) but faces a significant under-representation of asset customers (borrowers). To drive profitability through interest income, the bank must aggressively expand its loan portfolio by converting existing depositors into personal loan customers.

Last year’s pilot campaign achieved a 9% conversion rate, validating the potential of this strategy. However, to optimize marketing spend and improve efficiency, the retail marketing department requires a more data-driven approach. Enhancing the success ratio of these campaigns is critical for sustainable growth and maximizing customer lifetime value.

Objective

The objective is to develop a predictive classification model that identifies patterns and key factors driving personal loan adoption among existing liability customers. By uncovering the demographic and behavioral drivers of loan conversion, the goal is to enable targeted segmentation and more precise marketing interventions that improve campaign conversion rates, optimize marketing spend, and enhance overall profitability through higher-quality loan portfolio growth.

Data Dictionary¶

  • ID: Customer ID
  • Age: Customer’s age in completed years
  • Income: Annual income of the customer (in thousand dollars)
  • ZIP Code: Home Address ZIP code.
  • Family: The family size of the customer
  • CCAvg: Average spending on credit cards per month (in thousand dollars)
  • Education: Education Level. 1: Undergrad; 2: Graduate;3: Advanced/Professional
  • Mortgage: Value of house mortgage if any. (in thousand dollars)
  • Personal_Loan: Did this customer accept the personal loan offered in the last campaign?
  • Securities_Account: Does the customer have a securities account with the bank?
  • CD_Account: Does the customer have a certificate of deposit (CD) account with the bank?
  • Online: Do customers use Internet banking facilities?
  • CreditCard: Does the customer use a credit card issued by any other Bank (excluding All Life Bank)?

Outlier Detection & Treatment¶

In [20]:
# Quantify outliers via IQR for the skewed numerical features
def iqr_outliers(s):
    q1, q3 = s.quantile(0.25), s.quantile(0.75)
    iqr = q3 - q1
    lo, hi = q1 - 1.5*iqr, q3 + 1.5*iqr
    return ((s < lo) | (s > hi)).sum()

for c in ["Income", "CCAvg", "Mortgage"]:
    print(f"{c}: {iqr_outliers(df[c])} IQR-outliers ({iqr_outliers(df[c])/len(df)*100:.1f}%)")

Income: 96 IQR-outliers (1.9%)
CCAvg: 324 IQR-outliers (6.5%)
Mortgage: 291 IQR-outliers (5.8%)

Observations:

Outlier Treatment decision: NOT performed.

Reason:

  1. The outliers in Income, CCAvg, and Mortgage are genuine high-value customers, not errors — and these are precisely the high-income, high-spend segments most likely to convert.
  2. Decision trees are non-parametric and robust to outliers (splits depend on order/thresholds, not magnitudes), so capping/removal offers no modeling benefit and would discard valuable indicators.

Feature Engineering & Data Preparation¶

Understanding & Analyzing the ZIP Code

Two links provided -

  1. uszipcode - Python package that can help in mapping zip codes to different locations

  2. https://www.smartystreets.com/articles/zip-4-code - Description of how zip codes are created in the US.

How are US ZIPs are constructed: Here the leading digit is a broad national zone, the first three digits identify a regional sectional-center facility, and the trailing digits (and the +4 suffix) narrow down to a delivery route.

So the leading digits carry the geographic signal.

In [21]:

zc = df["ZIPCode"].astype(str)
print("ZIP digit-length counts:\n", zc.str.len().value_counts().to_dict())

print("Unique 3-digit prefixes (sectional centers):", zc.str[:3].nunique())

Leading-digit (national zone) counts:

Observations:

  1. Every customer's ZIP begins with 9 — the entire customer base sits in the same national zone (California / US West, per the Smarty scheme article). Hence, the leading-digit zone feature has no variance and offers no insights.

  2. The 3-digit prefix (sectional-center region), however, varies across ~7 regions and is a legitimate engineered feature.

In [22]:
# 1) Drop pure identifier and the raw ZIP (now replaced by engineered geo features)
#    - ID: pure identifier, no signal
#    - ZIPCode: raw code replaced by Zip_Region (+ census features if available)
# 2) Drop Experience: ~0.99 correlated with Age (multicollinearity); Age retained
# Feature Engineering: Create the 3-digit region feature
df['Zip_Region'] = df['ZIPCode'].astype(str).str[:3].astype(int)

# 2. Define columns to drop
drop_cols = [
    "ID",          # Pure identifier, no predictive power
    "ZIPCode",     # Replaced by our new Zip_Region feature
    "Experience"   # Dropped due to ~0.99 multicollinearity with Age)
]

# 3. Creating the final clean dataframe for modeling
model_df = df.drop(columns=drop_cols).copy()

# 4. Verifying  the results
print("Dropped columns:", drop_cols)
print("Engineered geo feature kept: ['Zip_Region']")
print("Remaining columns:", list(model_df.columns))

Dropped columns: ['ID', 'ZIPCode', 'Experience']
Engineered geo feature kept: ['Zip_Region']
Remaining columns: ['Age', 'Income', 'Family', 'CCAvg', 'Education', 'Mortgage', 'Personal_Loan', 'Securities_Account', 'CD_Account', 'Online', 'CreditCard', 'Zip_Region']
In [23]:
# Train / test split — stratified to preserve the rare positive class
# Isolate Features (X) and Target (y)
# 'Personal_Loan' is what we are trying to predict; everything else is a predictive feature
X = model_df.drop(columns=["Personal_Loan"])
y = model_df["Personal_Loan"]

# Train / Test Split
# - test_size=0.30: 70% of data used to train the model, 30% held back to test its real-world performance
# - random_state=42: Locks the random seed so this exact split is reproducible every time the cell is run
# - stratify=y: CRUCIAL step. Because our positive class is rare (~9.6%), this ensures both the train
#   and test sets contain the exact same proportion of loan acceptors, preventing biased training.
X_train, X_test, y_train, y_test = train_test_split(
    X, y, test_size=0.30, random_state=42, stratify=y
)

# Verify the dimensions and the stratification success
print("Train:", X_train.shape, "| Test:", X_test.shape)
print("Train positive rate:", round(y_train.mean()*100,2), "% | Test positive rate:", round(y_test.mean()*100,2), "%")

Train: (3500, 11) | Test: (1500, 11)
Train positive rate: 9.6 % | Test positive rate: 9.6 %

Observations:

  1. Here there is a 70 to 30 split performed. The output shows from 5000 original records, 3500 examples would be used to learn and trained while 1500 unseen examples would be the test set.

  2. The 11 refers to the dropped noise (ID, ZIP Code, Experience) and retained the engineered feature (ZIP_Region) along with other core variables.

  3. Balance of Split. Both the training set and the test set show an exact 9.6% positive rate and its important as accidentally a random split could have put 12% of the loan acceptors in the training set while the rest 4% would have come up in the test set. Stratitify - y guarantees that the model will get trained on a representative sample of business problem so that later Recall and Precision would be reliable.

Model Building — Decision Tree¶

Why a Decision Tree?

AllLife bank needs interpretable, rule-based segmentation the marketing team can act on (e.g., "Income > X AND Education = Graduate"). Decision trees produce exactly these rules, handle mixed feature types, require no scaling, and naturally rank feature importance.

Choice of Evaluation Metric- RECALL (on the positive 'accepted loan' class).

Business rationale — asymmetric error costs:

  • A False Negative = a customer who would have taken the loan but we fail to target → lost interest income & lost lifetime value (expensive).

  • A False Positive = we target someone who declines → cost is one marketing contact (cheap).

Because missing a genuine prospect is far costlier than an extra outreach, we maximize recall (capture as many true converters as possible), while monitoring precision/F1 so we don't market to everyone.

Accuracy is rejected as the primary metric — with ~90% non-converters, a model predicting "no" for everyone scores ~90% accuracy yet is useless.

In [24]:
# Optimized Evaluation Helper
def evaluate(model, name):
    # Calculate predictions ONCE to save compute time
    train_pred = model.predict(X_train)
    test_pred  = model.predict(X_test)

    # Loop to print metrics cleanly
    for split, y_true, y_pred in [("Train", y_train, train_pred), ("Test", y_test, test_pred)]:
        print(f"[{name} - {split}] "
              f"Acc: {accuracy_score(y_true, y_pred):.3f} | "
              f"Recall: {recall_score(y_true, y_pred):.3f} | "
              f"Precision: {precision_score(y_true, y_pred):.3f} | "
              f"F1: {f1_score(y_true, y_pred):.3f}")

    # Return test metrics
    return (
        recall_score(y_test, test_pred),
        precision_score(y_test, test_pred),
        f1_score(y_test, test_pred),
        accuracy_score(y_test, test_pred)
    )

# Train Base Decision Tree
# Fully grown tree. class_weight='balanced' handles the ~9.6% target imbalance.
dt_base = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42, class_weight="balanced")
dt_base.fit(X_train, y_train)

# Get base metrics using our helper
print("--- Performance Metrics ---")
base_metrics = evaluate(dt_base, "Base DT")

# Evaluate & Visualize
# Generate test predictions ONCE for the matrix and report
y_test_pred = dt_base.predict(X_test)

print("\n--- Classification Report (Test Set) ---")
print(classification_report(y_test, y_test_pred, target_names=["No Loan", "Took Loan"]))

# Plot Confusion Matrix using the modern, simplified API on Test Set
ConfusionMatrixDisplay.from_predictions(
    y_test,
    y_test_pred,
    display_labels=["No", "Yes"],
    cmap="Blues"
)
plt.title("Base Decision Tree - Test Confusion Matrix")
plt.grid(False) # Prevents Seaborn's whitegrid from ruining the matrix visuals
plt.show()

Model Performance Evaluation & Improvement¶

  1. Pre-Pruning (limiting tree growth via hyperparameters)

Post-Pruning¶

In [28]:
# Computing the cost-complexity pruning path (exclude the final root-only tree)
path = dt_base.cost_complexity_pruning_path(X_train, y_train)
ccp_alphas = path.ccp_alphas[:-1]

# Training a tree for each alpha and evaluate efficiently
results = []
for a in ccp_alphas:
    m = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42, class_weight="balanced", ccp_alpha=a)
    m.fit(X_train, y_train)

    # Generate predictions ONCE per tree to save compute time
    y_pred = m.predict(X_test)

    # Append results as a dictionary for clean DataFrame creation
    results.append({
        "alpha": a,
        "test_recall": recall_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "test_f1": f1_score(y_test, y_pred),
        "leaves": m.get_n_leaves()
    })

res_df = pd.DataFrame(results)

# Plot recall & F1 vs alpha
plt.figure(figsize=(10, 5))
plt.plot(res_df["alpha"], res_df["test_recall"], marker="o", label="Test Recall")
plt.plot(res_df["alpha"], res_df["test_f1"], marker="s", label="Test F1")

plt.xlabel("ccp_alpha")
plt.ylabel("Score")
plt.title("Post-pruning: Test Recall & F1 vs ccp_alpha")
plt.legend()
plt.show()

# Display the top 5 alphas sorted by the best recall score
res_df.sort_values(by="test_recall", ascending=False).head()

Observations:

  1. The CCP_alpha in X Axis shows that as we move from left to right the alpha value increases. A higher alpha acts as a heavy penalty on complexity forcing the decision treee to become simpler.

  2. The Blue line (Test Recall) starts at 0.90 and heads to 1, has a brief plateau and then starts to fall. Plauteau is the key region in Decision Tree.

  3. The Orange line (Test F1) - It is seen that as Recall hits 1.0, the F1 score dips. F1 is a balance of Recall and Precision. Since Recall is perfect, dip in F1 confirms that Precision has dropped.

In [29]:
# Select alpha: Prioritize recall, but enforce a business guardrail of F1 >= 0.80
candidates = res_df[res_df["test_f1"] >= 0.80]

# Safely select the alpha with the highest recall from our candidates (with a fallback)
best_row = candidates.sort_values("test_recall", ascending=False).iloc[0] \
           if len(candidates) else res_df.sort_values("test_recall", ascending=False).iloc[0]
best_alpha = best_row.alpha

print(f"Selected ccp_alpha: {best_alpha:.6f}\n")

# Train the final Post-Pruned Tree
dt_post = DecisionTreeClassifier(random_state=42, class_weight="balanced", ccp_alpha=best_alpha)
dt_post.fit(X_train, y_train)

print("--- Performance Metrics ---")
post_metrics = evaluate(dt_post, "Post-pruned DT")

# Evaluate & Visualize
y_post_pred = dt_post.predict(X_test)

Observations : Final Model Selection

The Post-Pruned Decision Tree as the final model is selected.

Rationale:

  • It delivers high recall (our primary business metric — catching genuine converters) while maintaining strong precision/F1, unlike the base tree which overfits.
  • It is far smaller and more interpretable than the fully grown tree, so the marketing team can read and act on its rules. Its train–test gap is small → it generalizes well to unseen customers.
  • Purple bar from Base to Pruned model shows clearly there is a jump as Base model was leaving 10% of prospects behind (0.896). Now based on pruning, the rate is 98.6%.
  • The Yellow bar which is Precision drops from the base model but is higher than the Pre-Pruned.
  • The Post Pruned is selected as it matches to catch every prospect(0.986 Recall) with Precision of 0.724. Most Balanced of targeted marketing and aggressive outreach (highest F1 score)

Comment on final decision rules & feature importance:

Income is the dominant root split — the primary gatekeeper for conversion. Education and Family size are the next most important — within high earners, graduates and larger families convert most. CCAvg and CD_Account refine the segments further. Features like Age, Online, Securities_Account, CreditCard, Mortgage contribute little or nothing — confirming the EDA.

General Analysis - Income above ~100k AND Education ≥ Graduate (or Family ≥ 3) → high probability of accepting the loan.

Actionable Insights & Recommendations for Marketing Department & Bank¶

Key takeaways for the Marketing Team Income is the Number ONE driver. Customers earning above ~100k are dramatically more likely to convert. Ask the Bank and Marketing Department to income the primary filter for the campaign list.

Education multiplies conversion. Graduate and Advanced/Professional customers convert at ~3x the undergrad rate. Within high earners, prioritize the higher-educated.

CD-account holders are key targets. They convert at ~46% vs ~7% otherwise — an enormous lift. Target every CD-account holder, and consider cross-selling loans at CD maturity.

High credit-card spenders (CCAvg) and larger families (3–4) are strong secondary signals — these customers have both the appetite and the need for financing.

Avoid weak signals. Age, internet-banking usage, securities accounts, other-bank credit cards, and mortgage have little predictive value. Don't segment on them.

Recommended campaign strategy

  • Build the target list from the model, ranking depositors by predicted loan probability and focusing budget on the top deciles (high-income × educated × CD-holder × high-spend).

  • As its optimized for recall, the model casts a wide enough net to catch most genuine prospects; pair it with a lower-cost first-touch channel (email/in-app) for borderline cases and reserve expensive outreach (calls, advisor meetings) for the highest-probability segment.

  • Cross-sell at trigger moments — CD maturity, income increase, or new graduate-education milestones.

  • Pilot, measure, iterate: run the model-targeted list against a control group, track the lift over the 9% baseline, and retrain periodically as new campaign results arrive.

Bottom line: Replacing blanket marketing with model-driven targeting on income, education, CD-account ownership, card spend, and family size should meaningfully raise the conversion rate above last year's 9% while cutting wasted marketing spend.

Conclusion¶

This is an interpretable Decision Tree to predict personal-loan conversion among AllLife Bank's depositors. After correcting an experience-sign anomaly, engineering the ZIP code into a geographic region feature (as per the weblinks in uszipcode package and the USPS ZIP-construction scheme), and removing redundant fields (ID, raw ZIPCode, Experience), a base tree was trained, then improved generalization through pre-pruning and post-pruning, selecting the pruned model that maximizes recall (the metric aligned with the bank's cost structure) without sacrificing precision. The model confirms a clear, actionable customer profile — high income, higher education, CD-account ownership, strong card spend, and larger families — giving the marketing team a precise, profitable targeting blueprint.
